heads.la: [cn: a | Ex iis est, quas synodi Romanae sub Bonifacio II gestis insertas Holstenius in prima parte Collectionis Romanae vulgavit. Cum Innocentius litteras istas episcopatus sui, quem statim ab Anastasii obitu iniit, primitias vocet; eas circa mensem Maium anni 402 scriptas fuisse non immerito colligamus.] EPISTOLA I, INNOCENTII PAPAE I AD ANYSIUM THESSALONICENSEM EPISCOPUM. Anysio Innocentius eam in Illyrici Ecclesias potestatem confirmat, quam Anastasius ejusque decessores ipsi concesserant.
heads.en: [nt: This is one of those letters which Holstenius published in the first part of the Roman Collection, inserted in the acts of the Roman synod under Boniface II. Since Innocent calls this letter the first-fruits of his episcopate, which he entered upon at once on the death of Anastasius, we may not without reason conclude that it was written about the month of May of the year 402.] EPISTLE I, OF POPE INNOCENT I TO ANYSIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA. Innocent confirms to Anysius that authority over the Churches of Illyricum which Anastasius and his predecessors had granted him.

heads.la: EPISTOLA II. E veteri exemplari Colbertino, not. 932.
heads.en: EPISTLE II. From an old Colbert exemplar, no. 932.

heads.la: EPISTOLA III. De [cn: a | Hunc titulum ac subsequentes e Sirmondo, non e mss. mutuati sumus.] dissensione corruptaque disciplina Ecclesiarum Hispaniae.
heads.en: EPISTLE III. On [nt: We have borrowed this title and those that follow from Sirmond, not from the manuscripts.] the dissension and corrupted discipline of the Churches of Spain.

heads.la: EPISTOLA IV. [cn: b | In edit. Concil. post 27. A Palladio in dialogo de vita S. Joannis Chrysostomi nobis transmissa est. Inde Romae inter epistolas Romanorum pontificum primum latine ex interpretatione Ambrosii Camaldulensis edita, post etiam graece in fronte epistolarum Chrysostomi cum nova interpretatione latina excusa est. Demum anno 1680, Emerici Bigotii studio cum toto Palladii dialogo castigatior et elegantior prodiit. Eamdem de integro ad mss. Coslinianum et Hamburgensem exegimus. Proxime post violentiam ecclesiae Constantinop. ab adversariis Chrysostomi in vigilia Paschae illatam, adeoque circa mensem Aprilem anni 404 scripta est.] JOANNIS CONSTANTINOPOLITANAE URBIS EPISCOPI AD INNOCENTIUM PAPAM.
heads.en: EPISTLE IV. [nt: In the edition of the Councils, after 27. It has been handed down to us by Palladius in the dialogue on the life of St John Chrysostom. From there it was first published at Rome in Latin among the letters of the Roman pontiffs, from the translation of Ambrose of Camaldoli; afterwards it was also printed in Greek at the head of the letters of Chrysostom, with a new Latin translation. At length in the year 1680, through the zeal of Emery Bigot, it came out more correct and more elegant together with the whole dialogue of Palladius. We have examined it afresh against the Coislin and Hamburg manuscripts. It was written immediately after the violence done to the church of Constantinople by the adversaries of Chrysostom on the vigil of Easter, and so about the month of April of the year 404.] OF JOHN, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE INNOCENT.

heads.la: EPISTOLA V. [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 34; quae autem 5 erat, nunc 68. A Palladio, cui uni debetur, paginae 24 dialogi de vita Chrysostomi sine titulo aut inscriptione inserta est. Ex interpretatione Ambrosii Camaldulensis inter pontificias epistolas latine Romae excusa, et exinde in editionibus conciliorum recusa fuit. Ejus scribendae occasionem ac tempus idem Palladius ibid. sic docet: Paucis post diebus, quam Innocentius a Theophilo per Alexandrinum lectorem accepisset, eidemque reddidisset litteras, rursum Theophili nomine in Urbem venerunt Petrus ipsius presbyter et Martyrius ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae diaconus, aliam Theophili epistolam cum quibusdam adversus Joannem gestis deferentes. Quibus perlectis Innocentius, cum nullas graves esse accusationes comperisset, novos illos legatos cum hac altera epistola dimisit. Unde illam non longo post superiorem intervallo scriptam esse colligitur.] INNOCENTII I PAPAE AD THEOPHILUM ALEXANDRINAE ECCLESIAE EPISCOPUM. Se a Joannis communione discedere non posse, nisi legitimo judicio damnetur. Theophilus ad canonicam synodum provocatur.
heads.en: EPISTLE V. [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 34; the one which was 5 is now 68. It was inserted, without title or inscription, on page 24 of the dialogue on the life of Chrysostom by Palladius, to whom alone it is owed. It was printed in Latin at Rome among the pontifical letters from the translation of Ambrose of Camaldoli, and from there reprinted in the editions of the councils. The occasion and the time of its writing the same Palladius teaches in the same place thus: A few days after Innocent had received letters from Theophilus by an Alexandrian lector, and had answered them, there came again to the City, in the name of Theophilus, Peter his presbyter and Martyrius, deacon of the church of Constantinople, bearing another letter of Theophilus with certain acts against John. When these had been read through, Innocent, having found that there were no grave accusations, dismissed those new legates with this other letter. Whence it is gathered that it was written at no long interval after the preceding one.] OF POPE INNOCENT I TO THEOPHILUS, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA. That he cannot withdraw from the communion of John unless he be condemned by a lawful judgment. Theophilus is summoned to a canonical synod.

heads.la: EPISTOLA VI. [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 3; quae autem 6 erat, nunc 39. In omnibus exstat omnium generum antiquis collectionibus, puta Isidori, Hispana, Hadriani I, Dionysii Exigui, Codicis a Quesnello vulgati. Eamdem exhibent codex Corbeiensis saeculo VI exaratus, Colbertinus majusculis litteris Langobardicis descriptus, etc. Ad haec anno 506 ab Agathensi concilio can. 9 laudata legitur. Quocirca ridet merito vir eruditus nec refutatione dignum censet heterodoxum quemdam, qui epistolam istam Innocentio hac una ratione abjudicari velit, quod Siricius in ea citetur. Quasi vero pontifice indignum sit, quod ipse definit, decessorum suorum a decretis firmare. Sed et Innocentio ea proposita erat quaestio, quae Siricii constitutionem ab ipso memorari necessario postulabat, ut sententiam suam adversus eos, qui aut scientes aut ignorantes peccassent, aequo discrimine moderaretur.]
heads.en: EPISTLE VI. [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 3; the one which was 6 is now 39. It stands in all the ancient collections of every kind, for instance those of Isidore, the Spanish, that of Hadrian I, of Dionysius Exiguus, and of the Code published by Quesnel. The Corbie codex written in the sixth century exhibits the same, and the Colbertine written in Lombardic capital letters, etc. Besides, in the year 506 it is read as cited by the council of Agde, can. 9. Wherefore a learned man rightly laughs at, and judges unworthy of refutation, a certain heterodox writer who would have this letter taken away from Innocent for this one reason, that Siricius is cited in it. As though it were unworthy of a pontiff to confirm what he himself defines by the decrees of his predecessors. But the question put to Innocent was one which necessarily required that the constitution of Siricius be recalled by him, so that he might temper his sentence with fair distinction against those who had sinned either knowingly or in ignorance.]

heads.la: EPISTOLA VII. [cn: f | In edit. Concil. 29; quae autem 7 erat, nunc 18. Descripta est ex Sozomeno, qui eam cum subsequenti epistola 12 e Latino sermone in Graecum conversam nactus, utramque lib. VIII, c. 26, edendam curavit. Inde ambas accepit postea Nicephorus Callisti, et libro XIII, c. 32 Historiae suae inseruit. Per hanc Innocentius litteris sibi ab eodem clero Germani atque Cassiani opera missis, adeoque anno 405 nonnihil jam procedente acceptis, rescripsit. Quippe, ut Palladius pag. 26 et 27 narrat, Romam advenerunt Germanus et Cassianus post Palladium, Palladius autem elapso mense post Cyriacum Synnadorum episcopum; qui quidem post legem anno 404, Novembris 18 die, Constantinopoli promulgatam, ex Oriente Romam confugere coeperat. Apud Sozomenum et Nicephorum inscriptioni Ἰννοκέντιος ἐπίσκοπος, etc., nihil praemittitur. Quocirca titulus in editionibus conciliorum ei praefixus, in quo ἀρχιερέως nomen Innocentio tribuitur, ut omni destituto auctoritate, nihil valet, ut usitatum tunc fuisse probetur ἀρχιερέως vocabulum. Idem dicendum et de epistola 12, in cujus titulo conciliorum editores et Innocentium ἀρχιερέα, et Joannem ἀρχιεπίσκοπον de suo appellant.] AD CLERUM ET POPULUM CONSTANTINOPOLITANUM. Eos ex ipsorummet sententia consolatus Innocentius, iniquam alterius episcopi in locum Joannis viventis subrogationem deplorat. Tum solos canones Nicaenos recipiendos, aliosque qui eis adversentur, repudiandos esse declarat. Demum significat sibi curae esse ut oecumenica synodus congregetur.
heads.en: EPISTLE VII. [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 29; the one which was 7 is now 18. It has been copied from Sozomen, who, having found it together with the following Epistle 12 turned from the Latin tongue into Greek, took care to publish both in book VIII, c. 26. From him Nicephorus Callisti afterwards received both, and inserted them in book XIII, c. 32, of his History. By this letter Innocent answered the letters sent to him by the same clergy through the agency of Germanus and Cassian, and so received when the year 405 was already somewhat advanced. For, as Palladius relates, pp. 26 and 27, Germanus and Cassian arrived at Rome after Palladius, and Palladius a month after Cyriacus, bishop of Synnada; who indeed had begun to flee from the East to Rome after the law promulgated at Constantinople in the year 404, on the 18th day of November. In Sozomen and Nicephorus nothing is prefixed to the inscription Ἰννοκέντιος ἐπίσκοπος, etc. Wherefore the title prefixed to it in the editions of the councils, in which the name ἀρχιερέως is attributed to Innocent, being destitute of all authority, is of no weight to prove that the word ἀρχιερέως was then in use. The same is to be said also of Epistle 12, in whose title the editors of the councils of their own accord call both Innocent ἀρχιερέα and John ἀρχιεπίσκοπον.] TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Having consoled them out of their own very judgment, Innocent deplores the unjust substitution of another bishop in the place of John while he lives. Then he declares that the Nicene canons alone are to be received, and that others which oppose them are to be repudiated. Lastly he signifies that it is his care that an ecumenical synod be assembled.

heads.la: EPISTOLA VIII. SEU EXEMPLUM [cn: a | In edit. Concil. post epist. 31. E vetusto bibliothecae Vaticanae libro in collectione Romana pontificiarum epistolarum primum prodiit. Nec immerito inter epistolas Innocentii collocata est, utpote cujus ille scribendae auctor praecipuus exstitit. Ut enim Palladius pag. 28 testis est, cum undique Romam confluerent sancti episcopi aliique viri religiosi, variarum ecclesiarum synodorumve de misero ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae statu litteras afferentes, non amplius sustinens pius pontifex, Honorium imperatorem de iis quae singillatim illae ferrent epistolae, certiorem fecit. Quibus ille motus, semel atque iterum, immo et tertio Arcadium, quid facto opus esset, missis litteris commonuit. Ex tribus illis epistolis prima excidit; haec secunda tantum latine habetur, tertiam graece Palladius, ex quo eam huic subjiciemus, nobis asservavit. A Baronio ad annum 404 haec refertur: sed ad annum 405, et quidem jam labentem pertinere, ordo rerum, quae Palladio teste eam praecesserunt, postulat.] SACRAE HONORII AUGUSTI MISSAE AD PRINCIPEM ORIENTIS ARCADIUM. Dolet Honorius de iis, quae in die Paschae Constantinopoli perpetrata sunt. Templi augusti et senatus incendium primum esse divinae iracundiae indicium. Alia metuenda esse nisi Deus placetur. Hac de re tacere se non posse, ne silentium pro assensu habeatur. Quam praepropere, dum episcopale judicium exspectabatur, in exsilium pulsi sint sacri antistites. Hinc religionis perturbationem inductam, et latum haeresibus atque schismatibus campum apertum esse.
heads.en: EPISTLE VIII. OR COPY [nt: In the edition of the Councils, after Epistle 31. It first came out in the Roman collection of pontifical letters from an old book of the Vatican library. Nor has it been placed without reason among the letters of Innocent, inasmuch as he was the chief author of its writing. For, as Palladius witnesses, p. 28, when holy bishops and other religious men were flocking to Rome from every side, bringing letters of various churches or synods about the wretched state of the church of Constantinople, the pious pontiff, no longer bearing it, informed the emperor Honorius of the things which those letters severally conveyed. Moved by which, he admonished Arcadius once and again, and even a third time, by letters sent, of what needed to be done. Of those three letters the first has perished; this second is had only in Latin; the third Palladius has preserved for us in Greek, from whom we shall subjoin it to this one. By Baronius this is referred to the year 404: but the order of the things which, on Palladius's testimony, preceded it requires that it belong to the year 405, and indeed when it was already drawing to its end.] OF THE SACRED LETTER OF HONORIUS AUGUSTUS SENT TO ARCADIUS, PRINCE OF THE EAST. Honorius grieves over the things which were perpetrated at Constantinople on the day of Easter. That the burning of the august temple and of the senate is the first sign of the divine wrath. That other things are to be feared unless God be appeased. That he cannot be silent on this matter, lest silence be taken for assent. How over-hastily, while an episcopal judgment was awaited, the sacred prelates were driven into exile. That hence a disturbance of religion has been brought in, and a wide field opened to heresies and schisms.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | Cum Honorius, Innocentii litteris provocatus, ad Arcadium de Joannis causa bis jam scripsisset, nec profecisset quidquam, petiit ab Innocentio sibi mitti episcopos quinque, presbyteros duos et diaconum unum, qui tertiam epistolam ad fratrem ferrent. Missi sunt Aemilius Beneventi episcopus, Cythegius et Gaudentius (forte Brixianus episcopus), necnon presbyteri Valentinianus et Bonifacius, ipse, ut videtur, qui Zosimo papae successit. Caeterorum nomina Palladius tacet, sed cum eis Constantinopolim profectos esse docet Cyriacum, Demetrium, Palladium et Eulysium. Epistolam hanc uni Palladio, qui eam dialog. pag. 29 inseruit, debemus acceptam. Latinam ejus interpretationem ex Ambrosio Camaldulensi repetitam Baronius ad annum 405 recudendam curavit. Circa vernum tempus anni 406 videtur scripta.] IX.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: When Honorius, provoked by the letters of Innocent, had already written twice to Arcadius about the cause of John, and had achieved nothing, he asked Innocent that five bishops, two presbyters and one deacon be sent to him, to carry a third letter to his brother. There were sent Aemilius, bishop of Benevento, Cythegius and Gaudentius (perhaps the bishop of Brescia), and also the presbyters Valentinian and Boniface, the same, as it seems, who succeeded pope Zosimus. The names of the rest Palladius passes over in silence, but he teaches that Cyriacus, Demetrius, Palladius and Eulysius set out with them to Constantinople. For this letter we are indebted to Palladius alone, who inserted it in the dialogue, p. 29. Its Latin translation, taken from Ambrose of Camaldoli, Baronius caused to be reprinted at the year 405. It seems to have been written about the spring of the year 406.] IX.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: e | Apud Dionysium sub titulo XXXVIII decretorum Innocentii exstat, sicut et in collect. Hispan. et Isid. Delata est per Germanum, qui cum Cassiano cleri ac populi CP. litteras, quibus Innocentius epistola 7 rescripsit, sub initium anni 405 Romae reddiderat. Probabile est, Innocentium vel hoc ipso anno 405 vel potius sequenti, ejusdem Germani opera usum esse, ut Aurelium et Augustinum salutaret, eaque occasione Germanum Africanis enarrasse quanta Joannes quamque indigna esset perpessus, et quae hanc ob causam Innocentio cum Theophilo discordia inter cessisset. Certe concilium Carthaginense anno 407 Junii 13 die celebratum, atque Cod. can. Afric. eccl. c. 101 relatum, ad Innocentium sibi scribendum decernit, quo Romanam inter et Alexandrinam ecclesiam pax componatur. Neque minus certum est Aurelium, circa idem tempus, suum erga Joannem studium patefecisse; qua de re ille scripta ad eum epistola gratias agit.] X. INNOCENTII I PAPAE AD AURELIUM GARTHAGINIENSIUM ET AUGUSTINUM HIPPONENSIUM EPISCOPOS, Salutatoria et plena charitate.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: It stands in Dionysius under title XXXVIII of the decrees of Innocent, as also in the Spanish and Isidorian collections. It was carried by Germanus, who with Cassian had delivered at Rome, about the beginning of the year 405, the letters of the clergy and people of Constantinople, to which Innocent answered by Epistle 7. It is probable that Innocent, either in this very year 405 or rather in the following one, used the services of the same Germanus to greet Aurelius and Augustine, and that on that occasion Germanus recounted to the Africans how great and how unworthy were the things John had suffered, and what discord had for this reason arisen between Innocent and Theophilus. Certainly the council of Carthage held in the year 407, on the 13th day of June, and reported in the Code of canons of the African church, c. 101, decrees that it should write to Innocent, so that peace might be composed between the Roman and the Alexandrian church. Nor is it less certain that Aurelius, about the same time, made plain his zeal toward John; for which matter he gives him thanks in a letter written to him.] X. OF POPE INNOCENT I TO AURELIUS OF THE CARTHAGINIANS AND AUGUSTINE OF THE HIPPONIANS, BISHOPS, Of greeting and full of charity.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: b | Ex editione operum Chrysostomi, ubi epistolis ipsius praemittitur, a Baronio ad annum 406, ut et a Pontificiarum epistolarum aut conciliorum editoribus repetita, a nobis autem ad vetus exemplar Hamburgense recognita est. Eam a se tertio exsilii anno, adeoque anno 407 scriptam esse Chrysostomus n. 4 testificatur. Exinde etiam sequitur, ut ante mensem Julium scripta sit, si Chrysostomus primum exsilii sui annum ab eo die, quo Cucusum perductus est, ad eumdem anni sequentis revolutum diem recenseat, non tertium vulgati computandi ratione a triplici consulum mutatione appellet.] XI. JOANNIS CHRYSOSTOMI EPISCOPI AD INNOCENTIUM PAPAM. Illius erga se paternum affectum et summam in rebus afflictis vigilantiam laudat, et ut hoc studium non remittat, iterum atque iterum obtestatur.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: From the edition of the works of Chrysostom, where it is set before his letters; repeated by Baronius at the year 406, as also by the editors of the pontifical letters or of the councils, but examined by us against the old Hamburg exemplar. Chrysostom testifies, n. 4, that it was written by him in the third year of his exile, and so in the year 407. From this it also follows that it was written before the month of July, if Chrysostom reckons the first year of his exile from the day on which he was brought to Cucusus to the same day of the following year come round, and does not call it the third by the common way of reckoning from the threefold change of consuls.] XI. OF JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, BISHOP, TO POPE INNOCENT. He praises his fatherly affection toward himself and his utmost vigilance in afflicted affairs, and entreats him again and again not to slacken this zeal. [n: (Hanc epistolam, ut aliam Chrysostomi supra memoratam, reperire potes tomo III operum ejusdem Doctoris.)]

heads.la: EPISTOLA XII. [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 28. Quae autem 12 erat, est Isid. Mercat. Epistolam hanc, sicut et superiorem VII, uni Sozomeno acceptam debemus. De utraque sic ille lib. VIII, c. 24, praefatur: Cum Innocentius oecumenicam synodum congregare studeret, scripsit ad Joannem, et seorsum ad clericos urbis Constantinop. Quibus verbis significare videtur, vel utramque epistolam simul missam, vel certe istam septima posteriorem non esse. Verum huic scriptori insolens non est, ea quae dissitis temporibus gesta sunt simul componere atque confundere. Sane cum de congreganda synodo, in qua Innocentius omnem spem posuerat, altum sit in hac epistola silentium, hoc non levi argumento est, eam scriptam esse cum ab hac spe excidisset. Istud non abhorret a vero, Innocentium proxima Joannis epistola motum, hanc scripsisse, ut sanctum praesulem in malis, quibus eum affligi didicerat, consolaretur. Quod si ita est, Joanni superstiti vix reddi potuit.] INNOCENTII PAPAE AD JOANNEM CHRYSOSTOMUM CONSTANTINOPOLITANUM EPISCOPUM. Joannem ob oculos posita patientiae commendatione consolatur.
heads.en: EPISTLE XII. [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 28. The one which was 12 is Isidore Mercator's. This letter, like the preceding VII, we owe to Sozomen alone. Of both he speaks thus by way of preface, book VIII, c. 24: When Innocent was striving to assemble an ecumenical synod, he wrote to John, and separately to the clerics of the city of Constantinople. By which words he seems to signify either that both letters were sent at the same time, or at least that this one is not later than the seventh. But it is not unusual for this writer to put together and confound things done at distant times. Certainly, since there is deep silence in this letter about assembling the synod, on which Innocent had placed all his hope, this is no light argument that it was written when he had fallen from this hope. It is not far from the truth that Innocent, moved by the last letter of John, wrote this one to console the holy prelate in the evils by which he had learned that he was afflicted. And if so, it could scarcely have been delivered to John while he survived.] OF POPE INNOCENT TO JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. He consoles John by setting before his eyes the commendation of patience.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In Romana synodo sub Bonifacio II olim recitata, subinde et a Nicolao I epist. 2 laudata, postmodum a Luca Holstenio cum caeteris praedictae synodi Romanae monimentis in lucem emissa est. Tempus, quo scripta est, consulari nota indicatur. Sed haec in nota mendum esse, ac pro Honorio IX et Theodosio V restituendum esse Honorio VII et Theodosio II clarissimus vir Tillemontius to. X, pag. 829, opinatur. Unde sequeretur, ut haec epistola anno 407 scripta esset. Hanc autem opinionem probare nititur ista inductione. Primo quidem statuit, ex epistolis, quas Innocentius ad Rufum scripsit, hanc primam esse, atque ab eo datam fuisse statim ut de Rufi ordinatione certior factus est; quod non negandum. Tum addit Rufum illum, ad quem Innocentius modo scribit, non alium videri ab eo, ad quem de Naissensibus clericis litteras jam dedisse se idem papa epist. 17, ad Marcianum, memorat. Quod pariter concesso, subdit: Atqui hanc epistolam ad Marcianum scripsit Innocentius Ravennae constitutus, quo ab anno 409 ineunte venit, et ubi mense Augusto anni 410 adhuc versabatur; nec ullum in historia vestigium, unde eum praeterea in eamdem civitatem rediisse conjectemus. Ex quo consequi putat, ut nec me Rufi ordinatio, neque epistola ista serius anno 408 differendae sint. Sed cum nequaquam omnia scripta sint quae contigerint, et qui Ravennam semel accessit, eo etiam secundo ac tertio potuerit pergere; cumque hujus rei, ipso viro clarissimo fatente, anno 413, quo frumentum Heraclianus Romam perferri prohibebat, causa et occasio non defuerit: minime tutum videtur certam epocham conjectura incerta mutare. Sane inusitatus valde foret is librariorum lapsus, ut cum in duorum consulum qui eamdem dignitatem gessissent pluries, annis exprimendis peccassent, eorum tamen error in eorum consulatibus designandis sic apte sibi cohaereret, ut cum Honorii nono consulatu, quintum Theodosii, non quartum aut tertium, ac vicissim cum quinto Theodosii nonum Honorii, non septimum aut alium quemvis componerent.] XIII. RUFO THESSALONICENSI EPISCOPO. Variarum ei committitur cura provinciarum, in quibus vicarius Innocentii et inter primates primus constituitur.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: Formerly recited in the Roman synod under Boniface II, thereafter also cited by Nicholas I, Epistle 2, it was afterwards brought to light by Lucas Holstenius together with the other monuments of the aforesaid Roman synod. The time at which it was written is indicated by the consular note. But the most illustrious man Tillemont, vol. X, p. 829, thinks that there is a fault in this note, and that for Honorius IX and Theodosius V there should be restored Honorius VII and Theodosius II. From which it would follow that this letter was written in the year 407. And he strives to prove this opinion by this induction. First, indeed, he states that of the letters which Innocent wrote to Rufus this is the first, and was given by him as soon as he was informed of Rufus's ordination; which is not to be denied. Then he adds that that Rufus to whom Innocent now writes seems to be no other than he to whom the same pope, Epistle 17, to Marcian, mentions that he had already given letters about the clerics of Naissus. Which being likewise granted, he subjoins: But Innocent wrote this letter to Marcian while staying at Ravenna, whither he came at the beginning of the year 409, and where he was still living in the month of August of the year 410; and there is no trace in history from which we might conjecture that he returned besides to the same city. From which he thinks it follows that neither Rufus's ordination nor this letter is to be put later than the year 408. But since by no means all things that happened have been written, and he who went to Ravenna once could also go there a second and a third time; and since, as the most illustrious man himself admits, a cause and occasion of this was not lacking in the year 413, in which Heraclianus was preventing grain from being carried to Rome: it seems by no means safe to change a certain epoch by an uncertain conjecture. Surely that slip of the copyists would be exceedingly unusual, if, when they had erred in expressing the years of two consuls who had borne the same dignity several times, their error nevertheless so aptly held together in designating their consulships, that with the ninth consulship of Honorius they joined the fifth of Theodosius, not the fourth or the third, and in turn with the fifth of Theodosius the ninth of Honorius, not the seventh or any other whatever.] XIII. TO RUFUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA. The care of various provinces is committed to him, in which he is constituted Innocent's vicar and the first among the primates.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: b | In Romana pontificiarum epistolarum editione notatur ut ex Cresconio descripta. Convenientius forsitan notatum esset ex Dyonisio. Apud hunc inter Innocentii decreta conficit titulum seu capitulum 50. Exinde illam et collectionis Hispanae auctor et Isidorus mutuati sunt. De paschali celebritate anni 414 in hac epistola disseri inter omnes convenit; ideoque illam anno 413 scriptam plerique censent. Verum Tillemontius subtiliter pro more suo expendens omnia, atque Pascha servandum ab Innocentio nondum praescribi, sed hunc papam prius, quam praescribere illud certo valeat, suam de eo sententiam Africana in synodo retractari, indeque ad se rescribi velle observans, anno 412 consignandam esse arbitratur: maxime, inquit, cum Aurelius et circa exitum Junii concilium provinciale, et circa finem Augusti plenarium Africae, in quo ex praescripto Carthaginensis III concilii can. 41 anni futuri Paschalis dies divulgandus erat, celebrare solerent. Nisi igitur synodum aliquam praeter consueta illa tempora in Africa celebratam cogitemus, eruditi viri opinioni videtur subscribendum. Alioqui non apparet qui Innocentius Africanae synodi de hac quaestione sententiam rescire, atque exinde totius Occidentis episcopis Paschae diem indicare commode valuerit. Ad haec, Leo papa de Paschali die anni 455 pariter sollicitus, ea de re non anno 454, quo dies ille ecclesiis praescribendus ac denuntiandus erat, sed ab anno 453 certior fieri pluribus litteris studuit.] XIV. De [cn: c | In mss. coll. Dion. et Hadr. aut simpliter de Pascha, aut de Pascha in qua re fallitur, hoc est utrum in ejus die praescribendo Innocentius fallatur, an non. In Hispan. de insinuatione vel indictis temporibus Paschae.] ratione Paschali anni 414.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the Roman edition of the pontifical letters it is noted as copied from Cresconius. It would perhaps have been more fittingly noted from Dionysius. With him it makes up among the decrees of Innocent title or chapter 50. From there both the author of the Spanish collection and Isidore borrowed it. That this letter treats of the Paschal celebration of the year 414 all agree; and therefore most judge that it was written in the year 413. But Tillemont, weighing everything subtly as is his wont, and observing that the Easter to be kept is not yet prescribed by Innocent, but that this pope, before he could prescribe it with certainty, wished his opinion about it to be reconsidered in an African synod, and a reply sent back to him from there, thinks that it should be assigned to the year 412: chiefly, he says, since Aurelius was accustomed to hold both a provincial council about the end of June, and a plenary council of Africa about the end of August, in which, by the prescription of canon 41 of the third council of Carthage, the Paschal day of the following year was to be made public. Unless therefore we suppose some synod held in Africa beyond those customary times, the opinion of the learned man seems to be subscribed to. Otherwise it does not appear how Innocent could conveniently have learned the opinion of an African synod on this question, and from there have indicated the day of Easter to the bishops of the whole West. Besides this, pope Leo, likewise solicitous about the Paschal day of the year 455, took pains by many letters to be informed about that matter, not in the year 454, in which that day was to be prescribed and announced to the churches, but from the year 453.] XIV. On [nt: In the manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections either simply de Pascha, or de Pascha in qua re fallitur, that is, whether Innocent is mistaken in prescribing its day, or not. In the Spanish: de insinuatione vel indictis temporibus Paschae.] the Paschal reckoning of the year 414.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: m | In edit. Concil. 13; quae autem 15 erat, nunc 20. Dionysius Exiguus epistolam hanc non indignam putavit, quam inter Innocentii decreta referret. Hanc sub titulo seu capitulo 39 proxime ante superiorem collocavit. Eumdem locum obtinet in coll. Hispan. et Isid. Forte cum eadem epistola missa est. Baronius scriptam opinatur anno 413, quo tacite refelleretur Pelagii liber ad Demetriadem Julianae filiam scriptus. Ad eamdem Julianam exstant epistolae Joannis Chrysostomi 169, Augustini 150, rursum Augustini et Alypii 188. Ipsi Augustinus anno 414 suam dicavit de Bono viduitatis lucubrationem. Ejus quoque Hieronymus in epistola 8, ad Demetriadem ipsius filiam, meminit.] XV. INNOCENTII PAPAE, AD JULIANAM NOBILEM EXHORTATORIA.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 13; the one which was 15 is now 20. Dionysius Exiguus thought this letter not unworthy to be reported among the decrees of Innocent. He placed it under title or chapter 39, immediately before the preceding one. It holds the same place in the Spanish and Isidorian collections. Perhaps it was sent with the same letter. Baronius thinks it was written in the year 413, so that the book of Pelagius to Demetrias, the daughter of Juliana, might be tacitly refuted. To the same Juliana there are extant letters of John Chrysostom, 169, of Augustine, 150, and again of Augustine and Alypius, 188. To her Augustine in the year 414 dedicated his work On the Good of Widowhood. Jerome also mentions her in Epistle 8, to Demetrias, her daughter.] XV. OF POPE INNOCENT, TO JULIANA, A NOBLE LADY, EXHORTATORY.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: b | In collectione Dionysii Exigui conficit haec epistola Innocentii decretum L. Titulus, quem ei praefixit idem Dionysius Exiguus, a Cresconio cap. 58 laudatur. Eam quoque Hispana collectio et Isidoriana exhibent. Ravennae se constitutum testatur Innocentius, dum illam scriberet. Eum autem in urbem illam circa annum 409 initio sese contulisse, ibique anno 410 cum ab Alarico capta est Roma, constitutum fuisse, Zosimus histor. lib. v, Sozomenus lib. ix, c. 7, et Orosius lib. vii, c. 39, tradunt. Unde per illud intervallum missam esse nonnulli opinantur. Alii anno 414 multo posteriorem arbitrantur, utpote in cujus exordio subsequentem ad Rufum, Marcianum et alios episcopos memorari existimant. Et eam forte ob causam in editione Romana rejecta est post sequentem, licet eidem a Dionysio praeponatur. Verum in sequenti epistola non de clericis Naissensibus, qui a Bonoso ante damnationem fuerant ordinati, recipiendis, sed de iis, quos idem haereticus damnatus ordinaverat, a clero repellendis agitur. Quocirca de tempore, quo haec epistola scripta est, nihil certi definiri valet. Hic tamen ad imitationem Dionysii non male ponitur: non solum quia subnexa probabiliter creditur anterior, sed etiam quia rerum ordo postulat, ut primum de ordinatis a Bonoso ante damnationem, ac deinde de ordinatis ab eodem post damnationem quid Innocentius sentiat, exponatur.] XVI. De suscipiendis clericis, quos Bonosus, antequam damnaretur, ordinasse cognoscitur.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the collection of Dionysius Exiguus this letter makes up Innocent's decree L. The title which the same Dionysius Exiguus prefixed to it is cited by Cresconius, cap. 58. The Spanish collection and the Isidorian also present it. Innocent testifies that he was stationed at Ravenna when he wrote it. And that he betook himself to that city at the beginning of about the year 409, and was stationed there in 410, when Rome was taken by Alaric, is related by Zosimus, Hist. book v, Sozomen, book ix, c. 7, and Orosius, book vii, c. 39. Hence some think it was sent within that interval. Others judge it much later, of 414, inasmuch as they reckon that the following letter, to Rufus, Marcianus and other bishops, is mentioned in its opening. And perhaps for that reason it was thrown back in the Roman edition to stand after the following one, although Dionysius places it before. But in the following letter the question is not of receiving the clerics of Naissus who had been ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation, but of repelling from the clergy those whom the same heretic had ordained after he was condemned. Wherefore nothing certain can be determined about the time at which this letter was written. Here, however, it is not ill placed, in imitation of Dionysius: not only because it is believed, with some probability, to be earlier than the one subjoined, but also because the order of the matter demands that we first set out what Innocent thinks of those ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation, and then of those ordained by the same man after his condemnation.] XVI. On receiving the clerics whom Bonosus is known to have ordained before he was condemned.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 22. Quae autem 17 erat, nunc 19.] XVII. Ex Dionysio Exiguo.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 22. And what was 17 is now 19.] XVII. From Dionysius Exiguus.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XVIII [cn: g | In edit. concil. 7. Quae autem 18 erat, nunc 21. Non in Mercatoris tantum, sed et in Hispana et Dionysii Exigui collectione exstat. Apud hunc inter Innocentii decreta locum 55 obtinet. Huc eam referimus, tum ne longius quae ad Macedoniae res attinent, disjungantur: tum maxime quia nec deest conjectura, unde illam cum de pace Antiochenae ecclesiae tractaretur, adeoque circa ann. 414 scriptam esse censeamus. Hunc quippe magno negotio Maximianum ex Macedoniae legatis unum interfuisse infra Innocentius epist. 22 tradit. Et haec forsitan praecipua causa fuit cur Maximianus iste ac socius moram in Urbe majorem quam sperabatur, facerent.]. De Bubalio et Tauriano damnatis a provincialibus episcopis, quorum sententiam sedes apostolica retractare curavit.
heads.en: EPISTLE XVIII [nt: In the edition of the councils, 7. And what was 18 is now 21. It is found not in Mercator's collection only, but also in the Spanish and in that of Dionysius Exiguus. With him it holds the 55th place among the decrees of Innocent. We put it back here, both lest the things which pertain to the affairs of Macedonia be disjoined further, and above all because there is no lack of a conjecture from which we may judge that it was written while the peace of the Antiochene church was being negotiated, and so about the year 414. For Innocent relates below, epist. 22, that this Maximianus, one of the legates from Macedonia, took part in that great business. And this perhaps was the chief cause why this Maximianus and his associate made a longer stay in the City than was hoped.]. On Bubalius and Taurianus, condemned by the bishops of the province, whose sentence the apostolic see took care to reconsider.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XIX [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 17. Quae autem 19 erat, nunc 21. In edit. Rom. notatur ut ex Cresconio descripta. Verius adscriptum esset, ex Dionysio, apud quem sub titulo XLIV decretorum Innocentii subjicitur.]. INNOCENTII PAPAE I AD ALEXANDRUM ANTIOCHENUM EPISCOPUM. De Pace. Quae Antiochiae propter pacem sunt gesta recolens, summa votorum potitus, communionem libenter concedit, eamque offert Acacio, modo et eadem praestet.
heads.en: EPISTLE XIX [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 17. And what was 19 is now 21. In the Roman edition it is noted as copied ex Cresconio. It would more truly have been ascribed ex Dionysio, in whom it is placed under title XLIV of the decrees of Innocent.]. OF POPE INNOCENT I TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH. On Peace. Recalling what was done at Antioch for the sake of peace, having attained the height of his wishes, he gladly grants communion, and offers it to Acacius, provided he too performs the same things.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XX [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 15. Quae autem 20 erat, nunc 41. Et haec epistola in edit. Rom. ex Cresconio notatur. Excerpta est potius ex Dionysio, a quo Innocentii decretum XLII nuncupatur.] INNOCENTII PAPAE I AD ALEXANDRUM ANTIOCHIAE EPISCOPUM. De Pace. Innocentius legationem ab Alexandro Antiocheno episcopo ad se destinatam sibi gratissimam fuisse missis gestis testificatur.
heads.en: EPISTLE XX [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 15. And what was 20 is now 41. This letter too is marked in the Roman edition ex Cresconio. It was rather excerpted ex Dionysio, by whom it is called Innocent's decree XLII.] OF POPE INNOCENT I TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH. On Peace. Innocent testifies, the acts being sent, that the embassy sent to him by Alexander, bishop of Antioch, was most welcome to him.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XXI [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 19. Quae autem 21 erat, nunc 17. Apud Dionysium, ex quo, non ut in edit. Rom. notatur ex Cresconio, epistolam istam accepimus, titulo XLVIII decretorum Innocentii subjicitur. Una cum duabus superioribus ad Alexandrum missam esse ex epistola 19 manifestum est. Neque minus est perspicuum eam apud Merlin. et Crab., ut in mss. coll. Hisp. ad Atticum Beroeae episcopum mendose inscribi. Nam Atticus Constantinopolis, non Beroeae episcopus erat. Quae ei a Dionysio, et exinde in collectionibus aliis ac vetustis concil. editionibus praeposita est summa, De sancto Joanne Constantinopolitano episcopo, non satis accurata, Acacium, cui inscribitur, praecipuas in depositione Chrysostomi partes egisse, ex Palladio passim, necnon ex Socrate lib. vi, c. 18, et ex Sozomeno lib. viii, c. 20, notum est. Is cum a Joanne neglectum se putaret, teste Palladio pag. 49 ira victus dixit: Ego ipsi ollam condio. Subinde idem Palladius pag. 82 Acacium una cum Antiocho dixisse memorat: Imperator, in caput nostrum sit Joannis depositio. Hinc, ut Theodorus diac. ibid. pag. 39 loquitur, et seditionis auctor, et delicti eorum, qui res novas Constantinopoli excitarunt, dux habebatur. Quapropter mediatore ac sequestro, cujus apud Innocentium non minor esset quam Alexandri gratia, indigebat. Neque sine causa Innocentius litteras communionis indices non ad Acacium ipsum, sed ad Alexandrum nonnisi certis conditionibus illi reddendas misit.] INNOCENTII PAPAE I AD ACACIUM BEROEAE EPISCOPUM. Qua conditione Acacio Innocentius communionem concedat.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXI [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 19. And what was 21 is now 17. From Dionysius, from whom, and not, as is noted in the Roman edition, ex Cresconio, we received this letter, it is placed under title XLVIII of the decrees of Innocent. That it was sent together with the two above to Alexander is manifest from epistle 19. Nor is it less clear that in Merlin and Crabbe, as in the manuscripts of the Spanish collection, it is faultily inscribed ad Atticum Beroeae episcopum. For Atticus was bishop of Constantinople, not of Beroea. The summary which was set before it by Dionysius, and thence in other collections and in the old editions of the councils, De sancto Joanne Constantinopolitano episcopo, is not accurate enough. That Acacius, to whom it is inscribed, played the chief parts in the deposition of Chrysostom is known from Palladius everywhere, and also from Socrates, book vi, c. 18, and from Sozomen, book viii, c. 20. When he thought himself slighted by John, as Palladius witnesses, p. 49, overcome by anger he said: I am seasoning a pot for him. Next the same Palladius, p. 82, records that Acacius together with Antiochus said: Emperor, on our head be the deposition of John. Hence, as Theodore the deacon speaks in the same place, p. 39, he was held both the author of the sedition and the leader of the offence of those who stirred up revolution at Constantinople. Wherefore he needed a mediator and go-between whose favour with Innocent should be no less than Alexander's. And not without cause did Innocent send the letters that were to signify communion not to Acacius himself, but to Alexander, to be delivered to him only on certain conditions.] OF POPE INNOCENT I TO ACACIUS, BISHOP OF BEROEA. On what condition Innocent grants communion to Acacius.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: g | In edit. Concil. 16. Quae autem 22 erat, nunc 16. Titulo XLIII decretorum Innocentii apud Dionysium, ex quo epistolam istam primum, non ex Cresconio habemus, subest. Ambigendum non videtur, quia Maximianus, ad quem scribitur, is ipse sit, cui ut et aliis Macedoniae episcopis Chrysostomus exsul factus epist. 163 gratias agit, quod ab ipsius partibus constanter stetisset, quique supra epist. 17 inter episcopos Macedoniae recensetur. Nec alius videtur ab eo Maximiano, Macedonum legato, qui in superiori epistola 18 Romae majorem, quam sperabatur, moram fecisse memoratur. Hujus autem morae probabiliter ea causa fuit, ut Romanae interesset synodo, et omnium quae in Antiochenae Ecclesiae reconciliatione acta fuerant, testis esset. Tum eorum, quae in hac synodo audierat, recitatione motus et animatus, statim ut Constantinopolim potuit pervenire, Atticum urgere, ut Antiocheni episcopi exemplum sequeretur, non destitit. Cum igitur ejus assensum utcumque elicuisset, moram, pati nesciit, quin ad Innocentium in gratiam ejus scriberet. Unde et huic papae epistolae hujus scribendae occasio data est. Quo tempore scripta sit, vel ex hac simplici expositione colligitur. Nam neque simul cum tribus superioribus, neque multo post conscriptam esse apparet: sed tantum inter hanc et illas cogitandum est intervallum, quantum opus fuit, ut Maximianus e Romana synodo Constantinopolim perveniret, atque inde litterae ejus in Attici gratiam reddi Innocentio potuissent. Quo pacto id quod desiderabat Innocentius ab Attico, Alexander in regiam urbem veniens impetrarit, Atticus ipse apud Nicephorum lib. xiv, c. 26, narrat.] XXII. DE ATTICO CONSTANTINOPOLITANO EPISCOPO. Communionem ei non reddendam esse, nisi prius eam legatione solemni rogaverit, et quae Antiochiae facta sunt ipse perfecerit, hoc est, in sacris diptychis Joannis nomen restituerit.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 16. What was 22 is now 16. In Dionysius, from whom, and not from Cresconius, we first have this letter, it stands under title XLIII of Innocent's decrees. There seems to be no doubt that the Maximianus to whom it is written is the very man whom, as also the other bishops of Macedonia, Chrysostom, when he had been made an exile, thanks in Epistle 163 for having stood constantly on his side, and who is counted above, in Epistle 17, among the bishops of Macedonia. Nor does he seem to be other than that Maximianus, legate of the Macedonians, who in the preceding Epistle 18 is recorded to have made a longer stay at Rome than was hoped. The cause of this stay was probably that he might be present at the Roman synod, and be a witness of all that had been done in the reconciliation of the Church of Antioch. Then, moved and encouraged by the recital of what he had heard in this synod, as soon as he could reach Constantinople he did not cease to urge Atticus to follow the example of the bishop of Antioch. When therefore he had somehow drawn out his assent, he could not bear delay, but wrote to Innocent on his behalf. Hence also the occasion of writing this letter was given to this pope. At what time it was written may be gathered even from this simple account. For it appears to have been composed neither together with the three preceding letters, nor long after them: but only so much interval is to be supposed between this one and those as was needed for Maximianus to reach Constantinople from the Roman synod, and for his letters on behalf of Atticus to be delivered thence to Innocent. By what means Alexander, on coming to the imperial city, obtained from Atticus what Innocent desired, Atticus himself relates in Nicephorus, book xiv, c. 26.] XXII. ON ATTICUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. That communion is not to be restored to him unless he has first asked for it by a solemn embassy, and has himself accomplished what was done at Antioch, that is, has restored the name of John in the sacred diptychs.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: f | In edit. Concil. 14. Quae autem 23 erat, nunc 3. A Dionysio sub titulo XLI decretorum Innocentii ordinata est, et in edit. Rom. non secus atque superiores, ut ex Cresconio notatur descripta. Bonifacius, ad quem scribitur, non immerito is videatur presbyter Romanae ecclesiae, qui cum presbytero altero et episcopis quinque ab Honorio ad Arcadium destinatus esse in Palladii dialogo p. 51 legitur, quique Innocentio post Zosimum successit. Tum forte legatione apud Theodosium pro negotiis apostolicae sedis fungebatur. Ex postremis verbis, quibus jubetur ut eos informet qui pro Attici partibus intervenire solent, epistolam hanc proxima ad Maximianum scripta non anteriorem esse liquet. Utramque simul missam jure opinemur. Huic simplex apud Dionysium et Isidorum praefigitur summa: De Antiochena ecclesia.] XXIII. De pace Antiochenae ecclesiae impertita.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 14. What was 23 is now 3. It was arranged by Dionysius under title XLI of Innocent's decrees, and in the Roman edition, just like the preceding ones, it is marked as copied from Cresconius. The Boniface to whom it is written may not unfittingly be taken to be that presbyter of the Roman church who is read in the dialogue of Palladius, p. 51, to have been sent by Honorius to Arcadius with another presbyter and five bishops, and who succeeded Innocent after Zosimus. Perhaps he was then discharging an embassy at the court of Theodosius on behalf of the affairs of the apostolic see. From the last words, by which he is bidden to inform those who are accustomed to intervene on the side of Atticus, it is clear that this letter was not written earlier than the one next to it, to Maximianus. We may rightly suppose that both were sent together. A simple summary is prefixed to it in Dionysius and the Isidorian collection: On the church of Antioch.] XXIII. On the peace granted to the church of Antioch.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XXIV [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 18. Quae autem erat 24, nunc 29. In edit. Rom. etiam epistolae huic communis cum superioribus apponitur nota, Ex Cresconio. Ipse Cresconius Breviar. c. 53 eam secundum divisionem a Dionysio inductam laudat. Is quippe tres in titulos, seu decreta, scilicet XLV, XLVI et XLVII, illam partitus est, decretis singulis praefixa summa, quam de more Hispanae collectionis auctor et Isidorus exscripserunt. Divisionem eamdem cum tituli seu capituli cujusque summa a Dionysio praefixa hic repraesentamus. Quamvis autem nullam haec epistola prae se ferat temporis notam, non videtur tamen superioribus sejungenda; maxime cum probabile sit, Alexandrum Innocentii epistola 20 invitatum ut ipsum litteris suis crebrius recrearet, oblatam amicitiam colere, et scrupulis, quibus movebatur, quam primum propositis utilem sibi efficere non distulisse.], AD ALEXANDRUM EPISCOPUM ANTIOCHENUM.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXIV [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 18. What was 24 is now 29. In the Roman edition this letter too is given the note common to the preceding ones, From Cresconius. Cresconius himself, Breviarium c. 53, cites it according to the division introduced by Dionysius. For Dionysius divided it into three titles or decrees, namely XLV, XLVI and XLVII, with a summary prefixed to each decree, which the compiler of the Spanish collection and Isidore copied out after their custom. We present here the same division, with the summary of each title or chapter prefixed by Dionysius. Although this letter bears no mark of its date, it does not seem that it should be separated from the preceding ones; above all since it is probable that Alexander, invited by Innocent's Epistle 20 to refresh him more often with his letters, did not delay to cultivate the friendship offered, and, by putting forward as soon as possible the scruples by which he was troubled, to make it useful to himself.], TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XXV [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 1. Quae autem 25 erat, nunc 50. Epistolam hanc exhibent Corbeiense exemplar saeculo sexto exaratum, et Codex a Quesnello vulgatus, necnon collectiones Dionysii Exigui, Hadriani Hispana et Isidori. A Dionysio appellatur epistola regularis, atque omnibus Innocentii decretis sub titulis octo, id est I, II, etc., ad viii praeponitur. Eam laudant tacito quidem Innocentii nomine concilium Hispalense II anno 619 habitum c. 7, Parisiense vi ann. 829, lib. 2, c. 27; illo autem appellato Isidorus Hispal. lib. II Offic. eccl. c. 26, Meldense concilium ann. 845 c. 44, et Nicolaus I, epist. alias 2, append. 2.]. Ex Dionysio Exiguo.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXV [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 1. What was 25 is now 50. This letter is presented by the Corbie exemplar written in the sixth century, and by the Codex published by Quesnel, and also by the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, of Hadrian, the Spanish and that of Isidore. By Dionysius it is called the regular letter, and is set before all of Innocent's decrees under eight titles, that is I, II, etc., up to VIII. It is cited, with Innocent's name tacitly passed over, by the second council of Seville, held in the year 619, c. 7, and the sixth of Paris, in the year 829, book 2, c. 27; with his name given, by Isidore of Seville, book II of the Ecclesiastical Offices, c. 26, the council of Meaux of the year 845, c. 44, and Nicholas I, epistle otherwise 2, appendix 2.]. From Dionysius Exiguus.

heads.la: I. [cn: b | Pro subnexis titulis, qui ex Dionysianis atque codicis a Quesnello vulgati exemplaribus describuntur hos exhibet vetus codex Corbeiensis. I. De pacem qualiter in ecclesia dare debet. II. De nominibus recitandis. III. De signandis infantibus. IV. De fermento. V. De baptizatis qui postea a daemonio vexantur. VI. De inunguendis infirmis.]

EPISTOLA XXVI. CARTHAGINENSIS CONCILII AD INNOCENTIUM. Ut sententiae suae, qua Pelagii Coelestiique impietates damnarunt, apostolicae sedis accedat auctoritas. Ac tandem si has illi suas esse negent; quibusvis earum assertoribus anathema decernitur.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXVI. OF THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE TO INNOCENT. That the authority of the apostolic see may be added to their sentence, by which they condemned the impieties of Pelagius and Coelestius. And finally, if those men deny that these are theirs, anathema is decreed against any who assert them.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XXVII. MILEVITANI CONCILII AD INNOCENTIUM PAPAM.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXVII. OF THE COUNCIL OF MILEVIS TO POPE INNOCENT.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XXVIII [cn: e | Ab Augustino lib. de Peccato orig. c. 9, et epist. olim 47, nunc 215, ad Valentinum, n. 12, haec epistola memoratur ut a quinque episcopis scripta. Quocirca quinque episcoporum non male in edit. concil. inscripta fuit. Ab eodem Doctore epist. olim 106, nunc 186, n. 2, ad discrimen superiorum, quae synodicae sunt, familiaris appellatur.]. EPISCOPORUM QUINQUE AD INNOCENTIUM PAPAM. Pelagii retegunt ac refutant haeresim, qua ad cupiditates domandas, tentationesque vincendas, necnon ad perficienda Dei mandata, solam sibi naturam humanam per liberum arbitrium sufficere contendebat: ac sicubi gratiam praedicaret, eum ibi vel liberum arbitrium, vel peccatorum remissionem, vel legis praeceptum intelligere, aliudque proprio gratiae nomine a fidelibus intelligi ostendunt. Quod item ait, hominem posse sine peccato esse si velit, quo sensu vere, quove, etiamsi non sine errore, tolerabiliter tamen dicatur, explicant.
heads.en: EPISTLE XXVIII [nt: This letter is mentioned by Augustine, book On Original Sin, c. 9, and epist. formerly 47, now 215, to Valentinus, n. 12, as written by five bishops. Wherefore it was not ill inscribed of five bishops in the editions of the Councils. By the same Doctor, epist. formerly 106, now 186, n. 2, it is called familiar, to distinguish it from the preceding ones, which are synodical.]. OF FIVE BISHOPS TO POPE INNOCENT. They uncover and refute the heresy of Pelagius, by which he contended that human nature alone, through free will, suffices for itself for taming desires and overcoming temptations, and also for fulfilling the commandments of God: and they show that wherever he preached grace, he understood by it either free will, or the remission of sins, or the precept of the law, and that something else is understood by the faithful under the proper name of grace. They also explain in what sense his saying that man can be without sin if he wills is said truly, and in what sense, though not without error, it is yet said tolerably.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: e | In edit. Concil. 24. Quae autem 29 orat, nunc 7.] XXIX. Innocentius episcopis Carthaginensis concilii rescribens eorum adversus Pelagianos haereticos doctrinam atque sententiam laudat et confirmat.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 24. And what orat 29 is now 7.] XXIX. Innocent, writing back to the bishops of the council of Carthage, praises and confirms their doctrine and judgment against the Pelagian heretics.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: k | In edit. Concil. 25. Quae autem 30 erat nunc in append.] XXX. INNOCENTII PAPAE AD CONCILIUM MILEVITANUM. Patres concilii Milevitani laudat, tum quod haereticos pertinaces segregandos, et correctos censuerint recipiendos, tum quod canones ubique receptos secuti, apostolicae sedis de rebus anxiis sententiam petierint. Inde probat haeresim, quae hominem sibi sine Dei gratia posse sufficere vult, ac baptismum parvulis ad vitam aeternam necessarium negat, contra Scripturas pugnare. Hujus auctores, eorumque sectatores ab Ecclesia abscidi jubet, sed si errores damnent, suscipi.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 25. And what was 30 is now in the appendix.] XXX. OF POPE INNOCENT TO THE COUNCIL OF MILEVIS. He praises the fathers of the council of Milevis, both because they judged that obstinate heretics were to be separated and the corrected to be received, and because, following the canons received everywhere, they sought the judgment of the apostolic see on anxious matters. Then he proves that the heresy which will have it that man can suffice to himself without the grace of God, and denies that baptism is necessary for little ones for eternal life, fights against the Scriptures. He orders its authors and their followers to be cut off from the Church, but to be received if they condemn their errors.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: f | In edit. Concil. 26. Quae autem erat 59, nunc 5.] XXXI. Rescribit Innocentius quinque episcopis, quid de eorum sententia, quid de Pelagii perfidia sentiret, se jam satis notum fecisse: haeretici hujus fautores, si Romae sint, latere; sed ubivis degant damnandos esse, eorumque saluti prospiciendum: Pelagii in Palaestina purgationem sibi valde esse suspectam; sed judices ejus nec culpare se, nec approbare; nihil opus esse ut eum Romam accersat, certe librum illius blasphemiis refertum esse: si ipse errores anathemet, facilius revocatum iri quos seduxit; sed his saltem consulendum.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 26. And what was 59 is now 5.] XXXI. Innocent writes back to the five bishops that he has already made sufficiently known what he thought of their judgment and what of the perfidy of Pelagius: that the abettors of this heretic, if they are at Rome, lie hidden; but that wherever they live they are to be condemned, and their salvation provided for: that Pelagius's clearing of himself in Palestine is very suspect to him; but that he neither blames nor approves his judges; that there is no need for him to summon him to Rome; that his book is certainly full of blasphemies: that if he himself anathematizes his errors, those whom he has led astray will more easily be recalled; but that these at least must be cared for.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: e | In edit. Concil. 27. Quae autem 32 erat, nunc 35. In veteribus Codicis a Quesnello vulgati nec non collectionis Isidori exemplaribus habetur, inscribiturque magno consensu epistola familiaris. Eodem tempore, quo tres superiores, scripta ac per eumdem episcopum Julium missa est.] XXXII. Aurelium Innocentius familiariter resalutat.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 27; the one which was 32 is now 35. It is found in the old exemplars of the Codex published by Quesnel and of the collection of Isidore, and with great agreement it is entitled a familiar letter. It was written at the same time as the three above and sent by the same bishop Julius.] XXXII. Innocent greets Aurelius again in familiar terms.
NOTICE ON THE THREE FOLLOWING LETTERS.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 34. Quae autem 33 erat, nunc 34.] XXXIII. Litteras Aurelio mittit Innocentius Hieronymo reddendas.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 34; the one which was 33 is now 34.] XXXIII. Innocent sends Aurelius a letter to be delivered to Jerome.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: c | In edit. Concil. 32. Quae autem 34 erat, nunc 33.] XXXIV. Innocentius Hieronymum, ob ea quae passus est consolatur, et quid pro tempore faciendum duxerit, ac jam fecerit, declarat.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 32; the one which was 34 is now 33.] XXXIV. Innocent consoles Jerome for what he has suffered, and declares what he has thought should be done for the present, and has already done.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 32.] XXXV. Joannem Hieronymum Hierosolymitanum prospicere debuisse, ne tot ac tantis malis, quibus afflictae sunt Paula et Eustochium, opprimerentur, ac nisi haec deinceps aut corrigantur, aut retundantur, rationem inde redditurum.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 32.] XXXV. That John Jerome of Jerusalem ought to have taken care that Paula and Eustochium should not be overwhelmed by so many and so great evils, by which they were afflicted; and that, unless these are henceforth either corrected or checked, he will render account for them.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: i | In edit. Concil. 9. Inter Innocentii decreta Dionysius Exiguus epistolae huic 37 locum tribuit. Eam inde sumpsit Hispanae collectionis compilator, ex quo et Isidorus, ut solet, eamdem exscripsit. A Cresconio c. 226 laudatur. Nullam prae se fert temporis, quo scripta sit, notam. Quapropter eam in classem epistolarum incerti temporis amandare cogimur.] XXXVI. Si maritus cujus uxor in captivitatem fuerat abducta, alteram acceperit, revertente prima, secunda mulier debet excludi.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 9. Among the decrees of Innocent, Dionysius Exiguus assigns the 37th place to this letter. From there the compiler of the Spanish collection took it, from whom Isidore too, as is his custom, copied the same. It is cited by Cresconius, c. 226. It bears no mark of the time at which it was written. Wherefore we are compelled to relegate it to the class of letters of uncertain date.] XXXVI. If a husband whose wife had been carried off into captivity has taken another, when the first returns the second woman must be excluded.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 4. In quinque titulos seu decreta XXVIII, XXIX, XXX, XXXI et XXXII, a Dionysio Exiguo divisa est. Citatur a Cresconio non semel. Exstat et in Hispana, ut in Isidori collectione.] XXXVII. 1. Si quis volens partem sibi corporis amputavit, clericus esse non potest; nolens autem potest. --II. Quod digami admitti ad clerum non possint. --III. Qui de laicis ad clerum non debeant promoveri. -- IV. Qui de laicis possint clerici fieri. Hic aperte concuba prohibetur. --V. De temporibus in cleri ordinibus immorandis.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 4. It was divided by Dionysius Exiguus into five titles or decrees, XXVIII, XXIX, XXX, XXXI and XXXII. It is cited by Cresconius more than once. It is found also in the Spanish, as in Isidore's collection.] XXXVII. 1. If anyone of his own will has cut off part of his body, he cannot be a cleric; but if against his will, he can. --II. That digamists cannot be admitted to the clergy. --III. Which of the laity ought not to be promoted to the clergy. -- IV. Which of the laity can become clerics. Here a concubine is openly forbidden. --V. On the times to be spent in the orders of the clergy.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: a | In edit. Concil. 5. Haec epistola in Dionysiana collectione, unde in Hispana et Isidoriana transcripta, locum obtinet, inscribiturque Innocentii titulus seu decretum xxviii.] XXXVIII. Ut ii, qui in presbyterio filios genuerunt, removeri ab officio debeant.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 5. This letter holds a place in the Dionysian collection, whence it was transcribed into the Spanish and Isidorian, and it is entitled title or decree xxviii of Innocent.] XXXVIII. That those who have begotten sons while in the presbyterate ought to be removed from office.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: e | In edit. Concil. 6. Collectioni Hispanae et Isidori inserta est secundum Dionysium Exiguum, qui eam sub titulo XXXIV decretorum Innocentii subjecit.] XXXIX. Quod post poenitentiam nullus ad clerum possit admitti.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 6. It was inserted into the Spanish collection and Isidore's following Dionysius Exiguus, who placed it under title XXXIV of the decrees of Innocent.] XXXIX. That after penance no one can be admitted to the clergy.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: i | In edit. Concil. 8. In collectionibus Isidori, Hispana et Dionysii exhibetur. Apud hunc decretum xxxvi Innocentii appellatur.] XL. In paroeciam alienam invadere, aut quidquam in ea, inconsulto ipsius episcopo, agere non licere.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 8. It is presented in the collections of Isidore, the Spanish and Dionysius. By the last it is called decree xxxvi of Innocent.] XL. That it is not lawful to invade another's parish, or to do anything in it without consulting its own bishop.

heads.la: EPISTOLA [cn: d | In edit. Concil. 20 Trium seu quatuor collectionum saepius nominatarum ope ad nos pervenit. Apud Dionysium praenotatur Innocentii decretum XLIX de Bonosiacis, quod Judaei sint comparandi. Quae summa exinde ab aliis canonum compilatoribus exscripta, cum in omnibus mss. tum in priscis edit. Concil. ac Rom. obtinuit. Immo ex hac summa et altera superioris epistolae 16 simul copulatis Cresconius breviarii sui capitulum 58 conflavit in hunc modum: De Bonosiacis haereticis, quod Judaeis sint comparandi. Et de suscipiendis clericis, quos idem Bonosus antequam damnaretur ordinavit. Ex decretis papae Innocentii tit. XLIX et L. Hinc factum, ut Merlinus geminum illum titulum epistolae huic praemittens, superiorem epistolam 16, tamquam hujus capitulum secundum ei subjecerit. Bonosi quidem Photinique, ut praevio in epistolam 9 Siricii Monito n. 7, observavimus, affines erant haereses; nihil tamen est cur a littera discedamus epistolae nostrae, in qua sectatorum Photini, non Bonosi, mentio occurrit. Immo si ad Seniensem in Croatia, seu, ut olim vocabant, in Liburnia, non ad Senensem in Hetruria episcopum haec epistola scripta est, Photini, non Bonosi asseclas in ea notari extra controversiam erit. Praeterea Photinum, cum Sirmii in Pannonia, cui Liburnia vicina est, episcopus esset, provincias illas haeresis suae veneno infecisse nemo ignorat. Demum Innocentio de haeresi sermo est, quam toto pene orbe disseminatam innuit, quod sane in Photinianam magis, quam in Bonosiacam recens obortam convenit. Ejus autem haeresis, quam Innocentius arguit, auctor dicitur Marcus, non quia illam excogitarit, sed quia seduliorem in ea propaganda operam prae se ferret.] XLI. Ut Laurentius haereticos Photini venena sectantes curet expelli.
heads.en: EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 20. It has come down to us by the help of the three or four collections so often named. In Dionysius it is headed decree XLIX of Innocent, on the Bonosians, that they are to be compared to the Jews. This summary, copied thence by other compilers of canons, prevailed both in all the manuscripts and in the early editions of the Councils and the Roman. Nay, from this summary and another of the preceding epistle 16 joined together, Cresconius composed chapter 58 of his breviary in this manner: On the Bonosian heretics, that they are to be compared to the Jews. And on receiving the clerics whom the same Bonosus ordained before he was condemned. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, tit. XLIX and L. Hence it came about that Merlin, putting that twofold title before this letter, subjoined to it the preceding epistle 16 as though it were its second chapter. The heresies of Bonosus and Photinus were indeed akin, as we observed in the preliminary Notice to epistle 9 of Siricius, no. 7; yet there is no reason why we should depart from the letter of our epistle, in which mention is made of the followers of Photinus, not of Bonosus. Nay, if this letter was written to the bishop of Senia in Croatia, or, as they used to call it, in Liburnia, not to the bishop of Sena in Etruria, it will be beyond controversy that the partisans of Photinus, not of Bonosus, are noted in it. Moreover no one is unaware that Photinus, when he was bishop at Sirmium in Pannonia, to which Liburnia is neighbouring, infected those provinces with the poison of his heresy. Lastly, Innocent speaks of a heresy which he intimates was spread through almost the whole world, which certainly fits the Photinian rather than the recently arisen Bonosian. And the author of the heresy which Innocent rebukes is said to be Marcus, not because he devised it, but because he showed more zealous effort in propagating it.] XLI. That Laurentius should take care that heretics following the poisons of Photinus be expelled.

heads.la: EPISTOLA XLII. SEU LITTERARUM PELAGII AD PAPAM INNOCENTIUM, POST MORTEM EJUS, SED CUM EUM DEFUNCTUM NESCIRET, SCRIPTARUM FRAGMENTA.
heads.en: EPISTLE XLII. OR FRAGMENTS OF THE LETTER OF PELAGIUS TO POPE INNOCENT, WRITTEN AFTER HIS DEATH, BUT WHEN HE DID NOT KNOW HIM TO BE DEAD.
NOTICE ON THE FRAGMENT FOLLOWING.[n: (Spicileg. Maii, tom. III.)]

heads.la: EPISTOLA XLIII. SEU FRAGMENTUM EPISTOLAE QUAM AD SEVERIANUM EPISCOPUM SCRIPSIT INNOCENTIUS UNUS EX PRIMIS ROMAE EPISCOPIS.
heads.en: EPISTLE XLIII. OR FRAGMENT OF THE LETTER WHICH INNOCENT, ONE OF THE FIRST BISHOPS OF ROME, WROTE TO BISHOP SEVERIAN.
